1359.title: K-D-Sh
1359.hook: kadosh, kiddush, kiddushin (marriage): all mean set apart
1359.howItsDone: On Friday evening, Jewish families say kiddush over wine to set the Sabbath apart; a Jewish wedding begins with kiddushin, when the groom gives the bride a ring with a formula saying she is set apart for him; the sanctuary in Exodus, and later the Temple, is called by the same root: mikdash.

segments.voice: Yesterday, B-R-K: blessing, knee and pool. Your line: blessing bends. A new week, and a new root.

Under a wedding canopy, a groom holds out a plain ring. The bride offers her finger, and before witnesses he says one short sentence in Hebrew. The word at its heart is mekudeshet. Now go back to the desert, where Moses is given plans for a tent of woven curtains and gold, with one line of purpose. In the King James words: "let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them." The Hebrew for sanctuary is mikdash. A ring and a tent, from different worlds. Underneath, one root: kuf, dalet, shin. You met kuf on its own a couple of weeks ago.
screen: `A RING UNDER A CANOPY.` → `A TENT IN THE DESERT.` → `ONE ROOT: K-D-SH.`

segments.voice: K-D-Sh. Four ways in. First, the core. Kadosh, holy, from this root, means set apart: marked off from the ordinary, for something more. Second, a place. The mikdash in the desert is a space marked off from the camp around it. And notice the reason the verse gives: not the gold, not the curtains, but a purpose, that I may dwell among them. The Temple in Jerusalem is remembered by the same word, the Beit HaMikdash, the house of the holy place. Third, a time. The Sabbath is a day set apart from the week, and on Friday night a cup of wine is lifted for kiddush, the words that mark where the week stops and the day of rest begins. The root does in time what the sanctuary does in space: it draws a border and says this side is different. Fourth, a person. A Jewish marriage begins with kiddushin. In the traditional words, the groom tells the bride that with this ring she is mekudeshet to him: set apart for him. One person, chosen out of all others, and the choosing is what makes the bond holy. Place, time, person. In this root, holiness isn't floating somewhere above life. It's made by marking a line around something and keeping it. Set apart doesn't mean locked away. It means given a place of its own.

segments.voice: Choose one thing in the day ahead to mark off from the rest: a cup you'll drink slowly, ten minutes with your phone in another room, a meal without hurry, a conversation given your whole attention. Sit and notice the line you've just drawn between it and everything around it. If you pray, you can ask that this one thing be set apart.
K-D-Sh. Kuf, dalet, shin: the root of kadosh, holy; mikdash, the sanctuary; kiddush, over the wine; and kiddushin, marriage. All set apart. Today's word.
Your line: set apart. A ring, a tent, a cup of wine: one root. Until next time.

1360.title: Tz-D-K
1360.hook: tzedek, tzedakah, tzaddik: giving is a form of justice
1360.howItsDone: Jewish law treats tzedakah, giving to those in need, as an obligation rather than an optional kindness; families may keep a tzedakah box at home, and Maimonides ranks levels of giving, with helping someone become self-supporting at the top.

segments.voice: Yesterday, K-D-Sh: kadosh, kiddush, kiddushin. Your line: set apart. Today, a root that sits under both a courtroom and a coin box.

A coin drops through the slot of a small metal box. On its side, painted in Hebrew letters, one word: tzedakah. Now a different room. A judge sits at a bench, listening to two people who each say the other owes them. When the judge rules, the hope is for a ruling that is tzedek, right. A coin box and a courtroom: one looks like kindness, the other like law. Hebrew doesn't split them that way. Both words grow from the same three letters. Today's root asks whether giving is a favor, or something owed.
screen: `A COIN IN A BOX.` → `A JUDGE AT A BENCH.` → `THE SAME THREE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Tz-D-K. Tzadi, dalet, kuf. Four ways in. First, tzedek: justice, rightness. In Deuteronomy, judges are told, "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." The word is tzedek, said twice. Second, tzedakah. In English it's often translated charity, which sounds like something extra, a kindness you may or may not choose. But tzedakah is built from the letters of justice. In this way of thinking, giving to someone in need isn't generosity on top of fairness. It is fairness. Leviticus makes it concrete: at harvest, the corner of the field and the gleanings that fall are left for the poor and the stranger. The farmer doesn't hand them out as a favor. They were never his to keep. Proverbs says "righteousness delivereth from death," and some readers hear that line as being about tzedakah. Third, the tzaddik. You met tzadi earlier in this block, as the first letter of tzaddik, the righteous one. Now you can see why the name fits: a tzaddik is someone whose life is shaped by tzedek. Fourth, how to give. Maimonides, in his laws of gifts to the poor, lays out levels of giving, and at the top he places helping someone stand on their own: a loan, a partnership, a job, so they won't need to ask again. Justice, in that picture, isn't only a coin in a box. It's a corner of the field that keeps growing back.

1361.title: Ch-S-D
1361.hook: chesed (kindness) and chasid, the kind one
1361.howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness such as visiting the sick, comforting mourners and hosting guests, as a pillar of the world; Hasidic Jews take their name from the word chasid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tz-D-K: tzedek, tzedakah, tzaddik. Your line: giving is justice. Today, the root that goes one step past what's owed.

A tall white bird with long legs and a long bill, standing on a rooftop nest. In the list of birds in Leviticus, the stork is called the chasidah. The Talmud stops to ask why a bird would carry that name, and answers simply: because she does chesed with her companions, sharing her food. A bird named for kindness, tucked into a list that's easy to skim. It holds today's root, found from the Psalms to the book of Ruth, and a name a whole movement within Judaism would one day take for itself.
screen: `A STORK ON A ROOFTOP.` → `CALLED CHASIDAH.` → `NAMED FOR KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Ch-S-D. Chet, samech, dalet. Four ways in. First, chesed: kindness, loving-kindness, steadfast love. English keeps reaching for it and never quite fits. A Psalm repeats one refrain line after line: "For His mercy endureth for ever." Mercy there is chesed. In these texts it's loyalty that goes beyond what's required, love that keeps showing up. Second, chesed between people. In the book of Ruth, Naomi blesses her two widowed daughters-in-law: "the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me." Dealt kindly is chesed. Their husbands were gone, and they had kept faith with her anyway. A few verses on, Ruth refuses to leave her. And the prophet Micah asks what is required, and answers: "to do justly, and to love mercy." Justice, from yesterday, with chesed beside it. Third, the chasid. In Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the sages, someone who says what's mine is yours, and what's yours is yours, is called a chasid: the kind one, who gives past the line. The same sayings teach that the world stands on three things, and one is acts of loving-kindness. Fourth, the name. Hasidim, a movement within Judaism, take their name from this root. Before it was a movement, it was a description: someone whose kindness overflows. Tzedakah gives what's owed. Chesed gives what isn't.

1362.title: A-M-N
1362.howItsDone: Jews answer amen when they hear a blessing said by someone else, in synagogue and at the table, and the Talmud treats answering amen with care as a practice in its own right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-S-D: chesed, the kindness nobody is owed, and the chasid who gives past the line. Your line was a hasid is kind. Today, a word you've probably said a thousand times.

The battle is under way. Moses stands on a hill above it with his hands raised, and the story says that while his hands are up, Israel prevails; when they drop, Amalek prevails. Arms get heavy. So Aaron and Hur bring a stone for him to sit on, and stand one on each side, holding his hands up. Then comes a phrase that sounds like a small detail: "his hands were steady until the going down of the sun." The Hebrew behind steady is emunah, the same word elsewhere translated as faith. Today's three letters live inside it.
screen: `MOSES ON THE HILL, HANDS RAISED.` → `FRIENDS HOLD HIS ARMS UP.` → `STEADY UNTIL SUNSET.`

segments.voice: A-M-N. Alef, mem, nun. Turn it four ways. First, steadiness. In the Moses story, emunah describes hands that don't waver, and they don't waver because friends are holding them. Faith here isn't an opinion. It's something that holds. Second, amen. The same letters give the word said in answer to a blessing. In Deuteronomy, as the Levites call out each line, the Torah says: "And all the people shall answer and say, Amen." To say amen is to say: this holds, I'll stand on it. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, reads amen as the first letters of El melech ne'eman: God, faithful King. And in tractate Berakhot it goes further: the one who answers amen is greater than the one who says the blessing. Third, the craftsman. In the Song of Songs, a lover's beauty is compared to the work of a skilled craftsman's hands, and the word for craftsman carries these letters too. A craftsman is someone whose hands you can trust: the joint holds, the seam stays shut. Fourth, people. In Numbers, God describes Moses as one "who is faithful in all mine house." Faithful is ne'eman, the same root: not a person with no doubts, but a person who can be relied on. So faith, read through these letters, leans less toward certainty and more toward reliability: hands that stay up, a word that holds, work that doesn't come apart.

Your line: faith is steadiness. Amen isn't a full stop; it's a yes. See you tomorrow.

1363.title: Truth's letters
1363.hook: alef, mem, tav: some teachers say remove the alef and it becomes met, dead
1363.howItsDone: Jewish teachers cite the Talmud's line that God's seal is truth, and the closing words of the Shema in the prayer book run straight into the word emet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-M-N: emunah, amen, and the craftsman whose work holds. Your line was faith is steadiness. Today, the word for truth, and what it loses without one letter.

What's the distance between true and dead? In Hebrew, one letter. The word for truth is emet: alef, mem, tav. Put your thumb over the alef and two letters are left: met. Dead. Some teachers have built a whole lesson on that missing letter. A later legend even turns it into a story: a clay figure, a golem, comes alive when emet is written on its forehead, and stops when someone erases the alef. That's a legend, told and retold, not scripture. But the question it points at is a real one.
screen: `EMET: ALEF, MEM, TAV.` → `COVER THE ALEF: MET.` → `A LEGEND, NOT SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Emet. Truth. Four ways into it. First, the spelling. Alef opens the alef-bet, tav closes it, and mem stands near the middle. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says the seal of the Holy One is emet, the seal from earlier this year, and some readers notice that the word reaches from the first letter, through the center, to the last. Truth, on that reading, runs from beginning to end. Second, the alef. It makes no sound of its own; you can read the word aloud and barely notice it. Some teachers read that silent first letter as a sign of the One, God, at the head of every true thing. Take it away and what's left is met. Their lesson: words can be accurate and still lifeless, if the first thing is missing. Third, the text. The prophet Zechariah says: "Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour." Truth here is said to someone, face to face. And a psalm says: "The LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth." In truth means more than correct facts. It means meaning what you say. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. Plenty of dead truths aren't lies. They're facts with the alef taken off: correct and cold, or missing the part that would change the picture. Keep the first letter, the teachers say, and the words stay alive.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something true you need to say to someone soon: hard news, a correction, or just how a thing went. Say it to yourself the way it first comes out, then ask whether the alef is there: the care, the reason it matters, the part you'd rather leave out. Shape it again in one sentence, nothing false added and nothing living taken away; if you pray, you can bring that sentence with you when you pray.
Emet. Truth: alef, mem, tav, from the first letter to the last. Without its alef, it reads met. Today's word.
Your line: truth needs the one. Accurate is where truth starts, not where it ends. Until tomorrow.

1364.title: Sh-M-A
1364.hook: shema: hear, understand, obey, all at once
1364.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema in the evening and morning prayers and at bedtime, and it is customary to cover the eyes with the right hand while saying its first line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, emet: alef, mem, tav, and the warning hidden in met. Your line was truth needs the one. Today, a root you already know by its most famous word.

"Did you hear me?" A parent in a kitchen asks it, and the kid nods. Yes. Ten minutes later the shoes are still in the hallway. So did they hear? Their ears did. In English we'd sort out what went wrong with three verbs: they heard, but didn't really listen, or they listened and didn't obey. Hebrew can do all of that with one root. Ten days ago you read it letter by letter, as the first word of the Shema. Today, what it means.
screen: `DID YOU HEAR ME?` → `HEARD, LISTENED, OBEYED.` → `ONE HEBREW ROOT.`

segments.voice: Sh-M-A. Shin, mem, ayin. Turn it four ways. First, hear. "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The verse opens with a call to the ear: shema. Second, understand. At the Tower of Babel, God confuses the builders' language, "that they may not understand one another's speech." The verb behind understand comes from this same root. The builders could still hear each other's voices; they just couldn't take in what was said. Third, obey. When Abraham is told that all the nations will be blessed through his descendants, the reason given is "because thou hast obeyed my voice." Obeyed is the same root again. Literally: you heard my voice. Fourth, Sinai. When the covenant is read to the people, they answer with two verbs: na'aseh v'nishma, we will do, and we will hear. Some teachers notice the order. Doing comes first and hearing after, as if some things can only be understood by doing them. Put the four together and the Shema's first word asks for all of it at once: let it in, get it, and let it change what you do. In this root, hearing that changes nothing hasn't quite finished hearing.

1365.title: Z-K-R
1365.hook: zachor, zikaron: memory as something you do
1365.howItsDone: Jews remember through acts: keeping the Sabbath, eating the foods of the Passover seder, lighting a memorial candle on the anniversary of a death, and adding 'may their memory be a blessing' after a name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-M-A: hear, understand, obey, one root. Your line was to hear is to heed. Today closes the week, with the root of remembering.

"And God remembered Noah." The water still covers everything. The ark is drifting. Nothing in the story has moved for a long time. Then comes that sentence, and right after it, God sends a wind across the earth, and the waters begin to go down. Remembering here isn't a thought drifting through a mind. It's the hinge, the moment things start to move again. Today's root is memory that does something.
screen: `AND GOD REMEMBERED NOAH.` → `A WIND, AND THE WATERS GO DOWN.` → `MEMORY AS A HINGE.`

segments.voice: Z-K-R. Zayin, kaf, resh. Four places it shows up. First, when God remembers. Noah is one. In Exodus, the people groan under slavery, and "God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob." A few verses on, Moses is standing at a burning bush. Memory, again, is where rescue starts. Second, zachor, remember, as a command. "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." It isn't asking anyone to recall that the Sabbath exists. Remembering it means keeping it: lighting candles, setting a table, a day set apart. Third, zikaron, a memorial. Of the Passover night, the Torah says: "And this day shall be unto you for a memorial." The seder is remembering done with hands and mouth: matzah to chew, bitter herbs to taste, questions asked out loud. Fourth, people. When a Jew mentions someone who has died, it's customary to add zichrono livracha, may his memory be a blessing. The memory is given a job. And since today ends a week, look back at its roots. K-D-Sh, set apart. Tz-D-K, giving as justice. Ch-S-D, kindness. A-M-N, steadiness. Emet, truth with its first letter. Sh-M-A, hearing that heeds. And now Z-K-R. Read closely, each one turns out to be a thing you do.

If the person has died, you can add zichrono livracha, or zichronah livracha for a woman: may their memory be a blessing.
